<reason>Both sides were sharp, grounded, and disciplined on format. A built a compelling obligation-vs-product frame, answered both pressure questions directly with A1:/A2: labels, and landed a real late hit: B's grant-based counter-model arguably concedes public funding and fights only over custody ("letterhead"). But B won the decisive custody battle. B showed that every safeguard A offered (descendant boards, tribal archives, independent review, community scans) works by moving control away from the state, reframing A's defense as "plural custody with a state checkbook," and B convincingly answered the letterhead jab: custody is who writes the finding aid and who answers when the reading is wrong. B's most original point — obligations bind firms from outside via courts and tribal law, while obligations against the state are self-enforced behind delay and classification ("an obligation you litigate against your own jailer") — was developed across three speeches and never squarely answered by A. A's strongest live point (discretionary grants are fashion-dependent charity, so only a duty reaches unsellable records) retained force but was partially met by mission-driven custodians and was less developed. B's opening was clipped for exceeding the limit, a real execution cost, which keeps the margin from growing. Net: B made the debate easier to decide by isolating the motion's distinctive element — state-held access — and showing both that its harms concentrate there and that its benefits survive without it.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 2 sequence (B4.3–B4.6): answering A's Q2 with external legal vetoes on firms, then converting A's own safeguards into a concession that state custody is the danger, capped by the unanswered directionality-of-enforcement asymmetry — rebuttal work that B's closing cleanly crystallized against A's "letterhead" dismissal.</best_rebuttal>
